exp: The question is vague and likely a poor translation; 'is its output' is the one statement that's unconditionally true of any computer-prepared graph, whereas 'hard copy' only applies if it's printed rather than shown on screen.
A speaker, joystick and plotter are all peripherals that take in or give out data (I/O devices); the ALU is an internal CPU component that performs arithmetic/logic, not an I/O device.
The set of parallel wires carrying data, address and control signals between the CPU, memory and peripherals is called a bus.
Memory that can only be read (not written during normal operation) is generically called ROM; PROM/EPROM are specific programmable variants of ROM.
An employee address is textual/alphanumeric data, not a number, unlike an exam score or bank balance which are both numeric.
A Winchester disk is the classic sealed hard-disk design with a fixed (non-removable) stack of rigid platters and heads enclosed together, as opposed to a removable or flexible (floppy) disk.
The CPU is the component that directs and coordinates all input, output, and processing activity in the computer.
The operation code (opcode) field of a machine instruction specifies what operation the CPU is to perform; the address/operand fields specify what data to operate on.

A DRAM cell stores one bit as charge on a capacitor accessed through a single transistor, which is why it needs periodic refreshing; SRAM instead uses a multi-transistor latch (typically 6 transistors) per bit.
In cutoff, both the base-emitter and base-collector junctions are reverse biased and essentially no collector current flows, so the transistor behaves like an open switch.
A 1-of-32 output decoder needs 32/8 = 4 of the 3-to-8 decoders as the output stage (each handling one group of 8 outputs, selected via a separate decode of the two extra address bits).

The options use mangled Symbol-font characters ('\uf03d','\uf02b') for '=' and '+', and more importantly the actual K-map diagram the question refers to was not captured in the extracted text, so there is no way to verify which grouping of cells is correct. Picking B (X = AB) only because it is the shortest/simplest expression among the choices, consistent with the question asking for the 'simplest' equation, but this is a guess.

Boolean algebra (algebraic manipulation) and Karnaugh mapping are the two standard analytical/graphical methods taught for simplifying logic circuits; trial-and-error or waveform analysis are not systematic simplification techniques.
A ring counter circulates a single 1 through its flip-flops, so it must be started by presetting exactly one flip-flop to 1 and clearing all the others to 0.
Sum = A xor B xor Cin = 1 xor 1 xor 0 = 0. Carry = majority(A,B,Cin) = majority(1,1,0) = 1. So S=0, Cout=1.

Standard TTL practice: unused AND/NAND inputs are tied to VCC through a pull-up resistor (so they read logic 1 and don't affect the AND function), while unused OR/NOR inputs are grounded (so they read logic 0 and don't affect the OR function); leaving inputs floating risks noise pickup.

ECL's defining traits are a small (low) output voltage swing and low noise margin, a negative power-supply convention, very fast switching speed, and correspondingly high power consumption -- this is the standard textbook summary of ECL versus TTL/CMOS.

All three precautions -- not inserting CMOS devices into a powered circuit, grounding tools/equipment/workbenches, and storing/shipping devices in antistatic packaging -- are standard ESD-protection practice for CMOS.

Swapping which transistor sits on which supply rail flips which terminal is the 'drain' by convention (drain = higher-potential terminal for an nMOS, source = higher-potential terminal for a pMOS); working through the new connections, the output node ends up tied to the source terminal of both transistors instead of the usual drain-drain node.

The standard DAC error types are offset error and (non)monotonicity error (along with gain/linearity error, not listed here); 'incorrect output codes' is a vaguer, non-standard label, so the pair that names genuine, specific DAC error types is nonmonotonic and offset error together.
If the comparator's inputs satisfy A>B, its A>B output line is driven to logic 1.
A silicon BJT needs roughly 0.7V of forward base-emitter bias to conduct; below that (in cutoff) Vbe is less than about 0.7V and the transistor stays off.
A PNP transistor used as a high-side switch supplies (sources) current from the positive rail out into the load, as opposed to an NPN low-side switch, which sinks current from the load to ground.
Stray (parasitic) junction capacitances must charge or discharge before the collector current can settle, which is what delays the transistor from reaching its steady-state current instantaneously.
De Morgan's theorem: (AB)' = A' + B' (and dually (A+B)' = A'B'); option A states this correctly, while B and C misstate the dual form.

Y = AB' + (A'+B)C = AB' + A'C + BC. Grouping by C: minterms with C=1 are exactly {A'B'C, A'BC, AB'C, ABC}, i.e. all of C, plus the C=0 term AB'C' from AB'. So Y = C + AB'C' = C + AB' (by absorption, XC'+C = X+C). Final: Y = AB' + C.
TTL circuits are built from bipolar junction transistors together with resistors (its name reflects multi-emitter input transistors driving an output transistor stage); it isn't diode-based like DTL.
Registers sit inside the CPU and are accessed in a single clock cycle, giving them the lowest (fastest) access time of anything listed -- far quicker than main memory or any disk/flash storage.
The minimum time between the start of two successive memory operations is exactly the definition of (memory) cycle time.

24-bit instructions occupy 3 bytes each, so instruction addresses must be 3 bytes apart starting from 300: 300 mod 3 = 0. Checking the options mod 3: 400 mod 3=1, 500 mod 3=2, 600 mod 3=0, 700 mod 3=1. Only 600 lands on a valid instruction boundary.

As stated, the premise is shaky: sign-magnitude, 1's complement and 2's complement all use the same fixed word length for a given machine, so none literally needs 'more memory' bits than the others. If forced to pick the representation most often criticized as wasteful, it's sign-magnitude, since it (like 1's complement) burns a code point on a redundant +0/-0 rather than gaining an extra representable value the way 2's complement does -- but this doesn't actually cost extra bits, so treat this pick as a weak guess against a flawed premise.
22 address bits address 2^22 = 4,194,304 words. Each word is 32 bits = 4 bytes, so total size = 4,194,304 x 4 bytes = 16,777,216 bytes = 16MB.
Numbers and encoded characters used as the operands of instructions are, by definition, data (as distinct from the instructions/opcodes that act on them).
The minimum time between the start of two successive memory operations is the memory cycle time by definition.
Buffer registers temporarily hold data being transferred between devices of different speeds, absorbing the mismatch so a fast device isn't held up by (or doesn't overrun) a slow one.
With several dedicated buses instead of one shared bus, more register transfers can happen in the same clock cycle, so fewer total cycles are needed to execute an instruction.
Pipelining overlaps the stages of successive instructions the way an assembly line overlaps work on successive products, so it's often called assembly-line operation.
In a synchronous system with fixed time slots, a unit that finishes early has no work to fill the rest of its allotted slot and simply sits idle until the next slot begins.

RISC's simpler, uniform instruction set needs less control logic and fewer transistors to decode and execute, which is why RISC designs (e.g. ARM) dominate power-constrained devices; ISA and IANA aren't architecture styles at all.
Devices chained A-into-B-into-C-into-the-computer's port, each plugged into the previous one, is the definition of a daisy chain.

Power MOSFETs are the device of choice for high-current switching because their low on-resistance lets them handle large currents efficiently with minimal conduction loss, which is why they dominate modern power-switching applications over plain BJTs.
A transistor's switching speed is limited chiefly by how quickly its junction (transition) capacitances can charge and discharge as it turns on/off.
The commutative law states A+B=B+A and A.B=B.A -- the order of the operands doesn't matter; the associative law is about grouping, not order.

y(x'z+xz') + x(yz+yz') simplifies as follows: yz+yz'=y, so the second term is xy. Expanding the first term gives x'yz+xyz'. Combining xyz' with the xy already found (xyz'+xy=xy) leaves x'yz+xy = y(x+z) = xy+yz. This doesn't match any of the plain single-letter options (x+y, x, y); option D's text is corrupted ('z i es') and was likely the intended (also mangled) correct answer before extraction damaged it, so this is treated as unresolvable from the given options.
